Stephanas
STEF-uh-nas
proper noun (figure)
Greek Stephanas (likely a shortened form of Stephanophoros, "crown-bearer," related to stephanos, "crown, wreath"). The head of a household that was the firstfruits of Achaia, addicted to the ministry of the saints (1 Cor 1:16; 16:15-17).

Biblical Definition

Stephanas was a Christian at Corinth whose household holds a notable place in the New Testament: it was "the firstfruits of Achaia" (the first converts of that Greek province) and devoted itself wholeheartedly to the service of the saints. Paul names him three times in 1 Corinthians. First, in the matter of baptism, Paul recalls, "I baptized also the household of Stephanas" (1 Cor 1:16) — one of the few he personally baptized at Corinth, and a household baptism that figures in discussions of who is included in the church. Second and most fully, near the letter's close: "I beseech you, brethren, (ye know the house of Stephanas, that it is the firstfruits of Achaia, and that they have addicted themselves to the ministry of the saints,) That ye submit yourselves unto such, and to every one that helpeth with us, and laboureth" (1 Cor 16:15-16). The word rendered "addicted" (Greek etaxan heautous, "they appointed/devoted themselves") is striking: the household of Stephanas had voluntarily set themselves to the unglamorous, ongoing work of serving fellow believers, and Paul urges the church to submit to and honor such devoted servants. Third, Stephanas was one of three men — with Fortunatus and Achaicus — who came to Paul (likely bringing the Corinthians' letter and gifts) and "refreshed my spirit and yours" (1 Cor 16:17-18), men whose service Paul says deserves acknowledgment. Stephanas thus models the devoted lay servant: not an apostle or a named office-holder, but the head of a household that gave itself to the constant, practical ministry of the saints, and was honored for it by the apostle himself. He embodies the truth that the church is held together not only by its appointed leaders but by the self-appointed devotion of ordinary believers who addict themselves to serving others.

Webster 1828 Definition

A Corinthian believer whose household was the firstfruits of Achaia and "addicted themselves to the ministry of the saints" (1 Cor 16:15); baptized by Paul (1 Cor 1:16); one of three who refreshed Paul's spirit (1 Cor 16:17); the model of the devoted lay servant.

STEPHANAS, proper noun. Greek Stephanas (related to stephanos, "crown"); a Christian of Corinth.

His household was "the firstfruits of Achaia" (the first converts of the province) — 1 Cor 16:15.

They "addicted themselves to the ministry of the saints" (devoted themselves to serving fellow believers).

Baptized by Paul personally (1 Cor 1:16); a household baptism.

With Fortunatus and Achaicus, came to Paul and "refreshed my spirit and yours" (1 Cor 16:17-18); the model of the devoted lay servant.

Key Scripture

1 Corinthians 16:15-16 — "I beseech you, brethren, (ye know the house of Stephanas, that it is the firstfruits of Achaia, and that they have addicted themselves to the ministry of the saints,) That ye submit yourselves unto such, and to every one that helpeth with us, and laboureth."

1 Corinthians 1:16 — "And I baptized also the household of Stephanas: besides, I know not whether I baptized any other."

1 Corinthians 16:17-18 — "I am glad of the coming of Stephanas and Fortunatus and Achaicus: for that which was lacking on your part they have supplied. For they have refreshed my spirit and yours: therefore acknowledge ye them that are such."

Galatians 6:10 — "As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith."

Modern Corruption

Stephanas is corrupted when the household baptism is pressed beyond what the text warrants in the credo-/paedobaptism debate, when his model of self-appointed lay service is forgotten, or when Paul's call to honor such servants is overlooked.

expand to see more

Household-baptism over-reading. The baptism of "the household of Stephanas" (1 Cor 1:16) is cited in the paedobaptism debate as possible evidence for the baptism of infants in a household. The text does not say whether the household included infants, nor whether any were baptized apart from personal faith; elsewhere the same Stephanas's household is described as having "addicted themselves to the ministry of the saints" (1 Cor 16:15), which describes responsible, serving believers, not infants. The Reformed Baptist reading holds that household baptisms in Acts and the epistles describe households of believers; the text of Stephanas, far from settling the matter for infant baptism, describes a household actively serving Christ. The dictionary holds the credobaptist position; the household of Stephanas does not overturn it.

Stephanas has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal point worth recovering is the model of the devoted lay servant: a household that voluntarily "addicted themselves" to the ongoing ministry of the saints, and whom Paul commanded the church to honor and submit to. The church is held together not only by its appointed officers but by ordinary believers who set themselves to serve. Paul's instruction — "acknowledge ye them that are such" (1 Cor 16:18) — rebukes a church culture that honors platform and overlooks faithful, unglamorous service.

Hebrew Roots

A Corinthian believer whose household was the firstfruits of Achaia and devoted themselves to the ministry of the saints (1 Cor 16:15); baptized by Paul (1 Cor 1:16); one of three who refreshed Paul's spirit; the model of the devoted lay servant.
